title: Weather Risk: Wind, Heat, Rain and Humid Flowering Conditions

content.overview: Outdoor weather creates short periods of elevated crop and worker risk. Wind, heat, heavy rain and prolonged humidity should be managed with forecasts, plant stage, structural support, drainage, irrigation adjustment and safe work practices rather than reactive guesses after damage occurs.

vocabulary.definition: The future time period covered by a weather forecast used for planning actions.
Bending or collapse of stems or branches from wind, weight or structural weakness.
A period of precipitation considered together with intensity, duration and soil conditions.

sections.title: Wind combines mechanical and water stress
sections.body: Strong wind can damage branches while also increasing evaporative demand. Structural support and irrigation planning should be evaluated before forecast wind events.

sections.title: Rain can shift root and disease conditions
sections.body: Heavy or repeated rain can saturate poorly drained zones and maintain wet plant surfaces. During flowering, prolonged wetness can increase disease pressure in susceptible crops.

sections.title: Heat affects both crop and worker
sections.body: High-temperature events can increase water demand and create occupational heat risk. Crop response planning should not ignore worker hydration, rest and safe scheduling.

workedExamples: Before a high-wind forecast, inspect trellis/support points and avoid assuming irrigation needs will remain unchanged.
After heavy rain, check low-field saturation before restarting the normal irrigation schedule.
commonMistakes: Continuing irrigation unchanged after significant rain.
Planning heat work solely around crop needs without worker safety.
content.practicalApplication: Review daily and multi-day forecasts, identify the crop stage and site zones most vulnerable, define pre-event actions and post-event inspections, and include worker safety in the same plan.
content.summary: Weather risk management is anticipatory. Forecasts become useful when they trigger defined actions for support, drainage, irrigation, disease observation and worker safety.
